content: Dental caries is a complex disease caused by the fermentation of dietary sugars by bacteria present in the dental biofilm, also known as dental plaque. This process leads to localized demineralization of the tooth surface, which can eventually result in the formation of cavities. Resin composites are commonly used in dentistry to restore teeth. However, these restorations can fail due to various reasons, including secondary caries, fractures of the restorative material, and other minor issues. Among these, secondary caries—defined as carious lesions that develop adjacent to restorations—are the primary reason for the replacement of restorations. The incorporation of antibacterial agents into both the filling material and the bonding systems used in composite restorations has been hypothesized to potentially inhibit the initiation and progression of caries near the restoration margins. This review represents an update of a Cochrane review originally published in 2009, aiming to evaluate the effectiveness of antibacterial agents in composite restorations for preventing dental caries. To achieve this, a comprehensive search of multiple electronic databases was conducted. These included the Cochrane Oral Health Group's Trials Register (up to July 23, 2013), the Cochrane Central Register of Controlled Trials (CENTRAL, Issue 6, 2013), MEDLINE via OVID (1946 to July 23, 2013), and EMBASE via OVID (1980 to July 23, 2013). Additionally, ongoing trials were searched in the US National Institutes of Health Trials Register, the metaRegister of Controlled Trials, and the World Health Organization International Clinical Trials Registry platform. No restrictions were applied regarding the language or publication date during the search. The inclusion criteria for this review were randomized controlled trials (RCTs) that compared resin composite restorations containing antibacterial agents with those that did not contain such agents. Two independent reviewers screened the studies in duplicate. Although no eligible trials were identified, the reviewers had planned to independently extract data and assess the quality of the trials using standard Cochrane Collaboration methodologies. A total of 308 references to studies were retrieved during the search. However, none of these studies met the inclusion criteria, and all were excluded from the review. Consequently, no randomized controlled trials were identified that evaluated the effects of antibacterial agents incorporated into composite restorations for the prevention of dental caries. The authors concluded that there is currently no high-quality evidence to support the effectiveness of incorporating antibacterial agents into composite restorations for caries prevention. This highlights the need for well-designed, adequately powered, randomized controlled clinical trials to address this gap in evidence. The conclusions remain unchanged from the previously published review, as no clinical trials were included in this update.
